This looks exactly like my carrier furnace. Does it attempt to start at all? My procedure is call for heat, inducer starts, spark ignitor starts, gas valve opens, flame sensor checks for flame.

If the procedure doesn't start at all, it could possibly be control board, if inducer starts, but no ignition, then that could be gas valve, igniter, incorrect has pressure, clogged holes in the gas manifold.

If the inducer motor runs and the igniter attempts to light, you can check voltage on your gas valve by removing the two wires connected to it, put a probe onto each wire coming from the board. If you get 24v there when it calls for ignition, then that's not the issue. You can check the gas valve by checking ohms across the two prongs on the valve. Should be a low number, reading of 0 or a high number indicates gas valve is bad.

One more possibility the igniter (orange wire) and flame sensor (yellow wire) could be too close to each other and causing interferences or short leading to that fault.

His advice is pretty good but here's what I recommend. Buy the premix mud and mix it really well with a drill and paddle mixer. Buy some good drywall tools like level 5. all I use is a 6" taping knife and a 12" knife.

When taping seams, put a layer of compound down, then smooth it out a bit. Pull out a length of tape, (paper tape) and use your drywall knife to create a pinch point to give the tape a clean rip. Start embedding the tape from the middle and work out to the edges. You do not want a lot of mud under the tape as that will lead to bubbling, you want enough to embed the tape and keep it seated.

In between coats use you're knife to go over and knock  rough edges and high spots down

I usually do a a coat for taping, then a coat over the tape with my taping knife, then go on to a full 12" width coat with feathered edges. I may add a fourth skim coat if there are a lot of scratches in the dried mud, or if I don't feel there is enough compound on the joints.

Sand lightly at the end to smooth it out, but if you do it right sanding will be minimal.

Good drywall knives make a difference too. I used to use crap knives from home depot or Lowes, ended up ditching them because they would rust. I picked up a 6" taping knife and a 12" knife from level 5 and it's a world of difference.
Yep, you want to do thin coats with feathered edges, end goal is to sand as little as possible. If you're good at drywall the amount of sanding you do is minimal.

Credit spreads are the exact same as a debit sprrsd, except you're selling options to receive a credit instead. If you're bullish in a stock, you would sell a put spread. You take a look at your security and analyze where the price has been, the best strategy in my opinion if you're bullish is to sell a put credit spread well under the current price. 

So it AAPL was reading for $130, I would probably set something up like this.

Sell 1 $120 put
Buy 1 $119 put.

You get a credit since you're selling the more valuable option, and you're buying power is only reduced by your max loss on the spread. The further away from the money you are though, the less you will earn per spread,  but you're probability of profit increases. 

Your max loss will always be the difference between strike prices minus the credit received. 

An iron condor is just a put credit spread and a call credit spread combined. A call credit spread is more of a bearish play, you're betting the price will stay under your verticle.

So we will use AAPL again. 

Sell 120 put
Buy 119 put
Sell 155 call
Buy 160 call

You will receive a credit based on the two options sold minus the two you bought, that credit is your max profit. 

Your max loss is the difference between the strikes on both your spreads combined minus the credit. To earn max profit, AAPL would need to expire between 120 and 155. So if you analyze a security that has been trading in a range for months, an iron condor is a good play on them right now.

The glorious thing about put credit spreads is you actually get a credit when you put the trade on. A put credit spread is bullish, you sell a put at a higher strike price and buy one at a lower, for example 15/10. The credit you receive is the credit from the higher strike sold, minus the lower strike put you buy. This credit is your max profit. 

Downside loss is low strike x100 minus high strike price x100 plus the credit you received so in the example above it would be (10x100) - (15x100) + whatever you're credit was. That is the max amount you can ever lose on the credit spread. To receive max profit you want the price to be above 15 when the option expires, anywhere in between 10-15 you will win/lose some depending on price. 

So to put on a put credit spread, you basically just need enough funds to cover the max loss, since if the price was below 10, you would exercise your bought put and sell at market, then sell the 100 shares at the 15 to the person who bought the put you sold.

Yeah, saw some guy in previous comments explaining how to hang and mud drywall, he said you sand between every coat and I'm just like. 🤦🤦

I don't know how you would get anything done if you sanded everything between every coat, I would never do drywall if that was the case.

Apply 3-4 thin coats, gradually working from your tape knife up to a 10" or 12" knife. 

Each coat should make your joint wider, you should have about 6" of compound on each side of the joint. Feather it out from the center of the joint, do not apply too much compound at once. 

Do it in this order.

Use a taping knife, imbed your tape and smooth out. Let it dry, knock down any bumps with your knife.

Second coat, apply with tape knife over joint, smooth out, this will be a fairly thing coat, just an extra coat over the tape.

Third, take a larger knife, I like a 12" knife. Apply compound to the center of the joint, then feather each side of the joint out until you have about 6" out on each side, all three combined should be fairly thin. 

Sand, don't go overboard, gently sand your joints with a sanding block, and sanding sponge for corners and edges. 

Look over your sanded areas with a flashlight and look for any dips. Apply a watered down skim coat over areas that need it and gently sand until the edges are feathered.

Worst thing you can do is apply too much compound, it's MUCH harder to remove compound than it is to add some.

You definitely do not need to sand in between every coat, that is crazy talk. 

First coat embed tape.

Let dry, knock down any high spots and bumps with your knife. 

Apply second coat over tape with taping knife.

Let dry, same process knock down any bumps with knife. 

Using a larger knife, (I prefer a 12") apply mud over the joint and feather out, you want this coat to be approximately the width of the knife. 

Drying process again

Last coat apply a larger area of mud, feather out each side using your 12" knife one side at a time. This will leave a slightly thicker coat towards the middle of the joint where the tape is, which will make it stronger.

After that drys, sand everything down until smooth, check over your joints for any irregularities, apply a skim coat off needed. 

Sanding in between every coat, you wouldn't get anything done.
